questions.question: Which of these best describes what an architecture team primarily does?
questions.explanation: A healthy architecture team amplifies other teams — guiding, connecting, and translating — rather than shipping the product themselves.
options: Writes the majority of the production code
Helps other teams make better decisions
Approves every pull request in the company
Picks the programming language for every project

questions.question: According to Gregor Hohpe, architects should sell ___ instead of issuing mandates.
questions.explanation: Hohpe's phrase "sell options, don't issue mandates" captures the idea that architects preserve flexibility by deferring commitments until they're necessary.
options: orders
options
diagrams
roadmaps

questions.question: Which is NOT a typical role of the architecture team?
questions.explanation: Architects guide and connect; they do not centralise all decisions. Empowering teams to decide is the point.
options: Connector between teams working on overlapping problems
Steward of cross-cutting concerns like security and reliability
Single approver of every tech choice in the company
Translator between business strategy and engineering

questions.question: In Hohpe's framing, what is the "strike price" of an architectural option?
questions.explanation: The "strike price" is the cost of exercising the option — i.e. how expensive it is to switch later. Good architects keep it bounded.
options: The cost to start a new project
The rework cost to change course later
The licence fee of the chosen technology
The time spent in design meetings

questions.question: Why do mandates from an architecture team often fail in practice?
questions.explanation: Premature commitment removes flexibility; teams routing around mandates is a symptom, not the cause.
options: Teams secretly dislike the architects
Mandates commit the organisation before the commitment is needed, and are often ignored or worked around
Mandates are always technically wrong
Mandates violate open-source licences

questions.question: An architect notices two teams are independently building almost the same service. The best first action is to:
questions.explanation: Connecting teams is a core architecture-team function. Mandates would override autonomy; ignoring it wastes organisational effort.
options: Order one of the teams to stop immediately
Connect the two teams and surface the overlap so they can decide together
Build a third version themselves
Ignore it — team autonomy is sacred

questions.question: Which book by Gregor Hohpe popularised the "Architecture Elevator" metaphor?
questions.explanation: Hohpe's "The Software Architect Elevator" frames the architect's job as riding between penthouse (strategy) and engine room (technology).
options: "Release It!"
"The Software Architect Elevator"
"Domain-Driven Design"
"Accelerate"

questions.question: What does it mean for an architectural option to "expire"?
questions.explanation: Options have an implicit expiry — scale, integration, or deadlines eventually force the decision to be taken. Good architects flag the expiry explicitly.
options: The licence of a chosen technology runs out
The moment the decision stops being cheap to defer — external pressure forces a commitment
A new architect takes over and cancels it
The option moves to a different team

questions.question: Which statement best captures the architect's output in Hohpe's model?
questions.explanation: Architects are leverage: their value shows up indirectly, in the decisions made by the teams around them.
options: The number of architecture diagrams produced
The quality of decisions made by the teams they support
The count of mandates published per quarter
Uptime of production systems

questions.question: What does "selling options" mean for an architect?
questions.explanation: Selling options means keeping decisions flexible — naming the trigger that will force a commitment rather than deciding prematurely.
options: Selling software licences to other teams
Deferring irreversible commitments until needed, and making it cheap to change course later
Providing multiple vendor quotes for a purchase
Offering different pricing tiers for cloud services

questions.question: Which cross-cutting concern is the architecture team typically the steward of?
questions.explanation: Cross-cutting concerns like security, reliability, and cost are not owned by any one product team — the architecture team stewards them across the organization.
options: Individual developer performance reviews
Sprint planning for each product team
Security, reliability, and cost — concerns that span team boundaries
Recruitment and hiring processes

questions.question: According to Gregor Hohpe, where does an architect's value actually show up?
questions.explanation: Architects work as leverage — their impact is indirect, appearing in the quality and speed of decisions made by the teams they guide and connect.
options: In the number of diagrams they produce
In the quality of decisions made by the teams they support
In the lines of code they contribute
In the number of mandates they publish

questions.question: What is the GUIDE role of the architecture team?
questions.explanation: The guide role is about expanding teams' awareness of options and trade-offs — not directing, but illuminating so teams can decide well.
options: Directing teams with binding technical decisions
Helping teams see trade-offs and options they might otherwise miss
Approving all technical choices before implementation
Managing the backlog of all technical tasks

questions.question: What is the CONNECTOR role of the architecture team?
questions.explanation: Connectors reduce duplicated effort and missed synergies by making sure teams with overlapping problems find each other.
options: Connecting cloud infrastructure components
Linking teams working on overlapping problems so they can coordinate and learn from each other
Connecting developers to job opportunities
Connecting business to vendor contracts

questions.question: What does the architecture team's TRANSLATOR role involve?
questions.explanation: Translation is a core architect skill: business and engineering speak different languages; the architecture team makes each comprehensible to the other.
options: Translating technical documentation into other languages
Bridging business strategy and engineering — converting between their different vocabularies
Translating user requirements into wireframes
Converting code from one programming language to another

questions.question: Which of these is something a healthy architecture team does NOT do?
questions.explanation: Centralizing all technology decisions defeats the purpose — it recreates the ivory tower. A healthy architecture team empowers teams to decide, not replaces their judgment.
options: Help teams understand trade-offs
Connect teams with overlapping concerns
Own all technology decisions centrally for the organization
Bridge business strategy and engineering

questions.question: An architect tells a team "you don't need to choose your message broker yet — but when you hit 10 k events/sec, that decision cannot wait." Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Naming the trigger ("at 10 k events/sec") and the action ("you must decide") is how architects keep options alive without making premature commitments.
options: Issuing a mandate about message broker selection
Selling an option — naming the trigger that will force a commitment while deferring it until needed
Suggesting the team should ignore the problem
Over-engineering by planning for 10 k events/sec immediately

questions.question: Why do architecture team mandates "often get ignored or worked around," according to Hohpe?
questions.explanation: When a mandate removes genuinely needed flexibility, teams find workarounds. The issue is premature commitment, not team culture.
options: Teams are lazy or disrespectful of authority
Mandates commit before the commitment is needed and remove flexibility, so teams route around them when they cause friction
Mandates are always technically wrong
Teams prefer to make decisions themselves for ego reasons

questions.question: What does "the team writes the code; the architect keeps the option space alive" mean in practice?
questions.explanation: Division of labour: teams deliver features; architects ensure the decisions those features depend on are made at the right time with full information.
options: Architects refuse to take any implementation responsibility
Architects focus on maintaining flexibility and pointing out consequences while teams make day-to-day implementation decisions
Architects review all code before merge
Teams don't need architects if they write good code

questions.question: Two teams are independently building near-identical customer notification services. The architecture team's best first action is to:
questions.explanation: The connector role surfaces overlaps. Letting teams see each other's work and decide for themselves preserves autonomy while eliminating blind duplication.
options: Order one team to stop building immediately
Build a third shared notification service themselves
Connect the two teams to surface the overlap and let them decide together how to align
Ignore it — team autonomy is more important than efficiency

questions.question: In Hohpe's framing, what is the "expiry" of an architectural option?
questions.explanation: Options have an implicit expiry: conditions that make the decision unavoidable. Good architects name this trigger explicitly so teams aren't surprised.
options: The moment the software license expires
The moment the decision becomes too expensive to defer — scale, integrations, or deadlines force a commitment
When the architect leaves the organization
When a new technology makes the old choice obsolete automatically

questions.question: A team asks "which database should we use?" The architect responds by presenting three options with trade-offs and the conditions under which each is optimal. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Presenting options with trade-offs enables an informed decision by the team closest to the problem — rather than imposing a potentially premature commitment.
options: Passing the buck to the team
Selling options — helping the team make a well-informed decision rather than imposing one choice
Avoiding commitment irresponsibly
Being indecisive under pressure

questions.question: What makes an architectural option different from simple indecision?
questions.explanation: Managing options means explicitly tracking what can be deferred, when it must be decided, and what it will cost to change — indecision is the absence of that management.
options: They look identical from the outside
An option is an explicit, named flexibility with a known trigger and bounded cost to exercise; indecision is an unmanaged unknown
Options are written down; indecision isn't
Options always involve financial instruments

questions.question: In Hohpe's finance analogy, the "strike price" of an architectural option is the cost to:
questions.explanation: The strike price is what you pay when you exercise the option: the rework cost of switching course. Good architects keep it bounded and known.
options: Buy a software licence
Change course later — the rework cost if the deferred decision is eventually exercised
Start a new project from scratch
Hire an architect to make the decision

questions.question: Hohpe's deep dive says architects "work to keep options cheap to exercise." What does this mean concretely?
questions.explanation: Keeping options cheap means reducing coupling and designing for replaceability — so when the trigger fires, exercising the option doesn't break everything.
options: Buy cheap software licences up front
Design systems so that switching a key component later doesn't require a massive rewrite
Avoid all irreversible decisions permanently
Hire cheaper developers who are more flexible

questions.question: "Architects collaborate with rather than command teams." According to the deep dive, why is this more effective?
questions.explanation: Mandates that bypass team buy-in get ignored or worked around. Options and informed guidance produce decisions teams own and execute well.
options: It avoids HR complaints about workplace culture
Command-and-control architecture produces mandates teams route around; collaboration produces informed decisions teams own and execute
Collaboration is always faster than issuing mandates
Teams are always more technically competent than architects

questions.question: Which paper, linked in the architecture-team info content, asks "Who Needs an Architect?"
questions.explanation: Martin Fowler's "Who Needs an Architect?" challenges and reframes what architects actually do in modern software development.
options: A paper by Kent Beck
A paper by Martin Fowler
A paper by Gregor Hohpe
A paper by Sam Newman

questions.question: According to Hohpe's options framing, why is it valuable to explicitly name the trigger that forces a decision?
questions.explanation: Naming the trigger prevents both under- and over-committing. Teams know exactly when they must decide, so they can prepare without premature optimization.
options: It gives architects credit for predicting the future
It prevents teams from deciding too early (before needed) or too late (surprise rework cost)
It satisfies audit requirements
It allows decisions to be automated

questions.question: An option has a "strike price" of six months of rework. The trigger is "when we integrate with System X." What should the architect do?
questions.explanation: Defer until the trigger fires. Deciding before the trigger wastes optionality; ignoring the trigger risks a surprise commitment cost when it arrives.
options: Make the integration decision now to avoid the rework cost
Defer the decision until integration with System X becomes a real requirement, then decide with full information
Avoid integrating with System X entirely to preserve the option indefinitely
Delegate the decision to the team with no further tracking

questions.question: The deep dive says the architect's job is to ensure "the cost of changing course later is bounded." What happens when this is neglected?
questions.explanation: Unbounded rework cost is the architectural equivalent of unmanaged debt: invisible until it must be paid, and potentially existential when it arrives.
options: Architecture diagrams become outdated
Decisions are made with hidden costs — the rework price of reversing them is unknown and potentially enormous
Teams gain too much flexibility
Architects lose influence over time

questions.question: Who created the C4 model?
questions.explanation: Simon Brown created C4 as a lightweight way to describe software architecture at different levels of abstraction.
options: Martin Fowler
Simon Brown
Eric Evans
Gregor Hohpe

questions.question: What are the four levels of the C4 model, from highest to lowest?
questions.explanation: Context → Containers → Components → Code. Each step zooms in one level.
options: Class, Container, Component, Context
Context, Container, Component, Code
Code, Component, Container, Context
System, Service, Module, Method

questions.question: In C4, a "container" is best described as:
questions.explanation: A C4 container is simply "a thing that runs" — a web app, a SPA, a job, or a database are all containers. Not specifically Docker.
options: A Docker container, specifically
A deployable or executable unit (app, service, database)
A UML package
A folder on disk

questions.question: Most teams using C4 day-to-day rely on which diagrams most often?
questions.explanation: Context and Container diagrams answer most conversations. Component is occasional; Code is usually skipped.
options: Only the Code level
The Context and Container diagrams
All four levels equally
Component and Code only

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about C4 notation?
questions.explanation: C4 is deliberately NOT UML — it trades formality for readability. A simple legend is enough.
options: C4 is a strict UML profile
C4 favours plain readability over formal notation; a legend explains colours and shapes
C4 requires at least ten shape types per diagram
C4 diagrams must be drawn in Visio

questions.question: What problem do "diagrams as code" tools like Structurizr solve for C4 adoption?
questions.explanation: Diagrams-as-code puts the diagram in the repo, tied to the code, so it stays current instead of going stale in a wiki.
options: They replace the need for any diagrams at all
They keep diagrams version-controlled and regenerable from a single source, so they don't silently rot
They make diagrams harder to share
They remove the need for a legend

questions.question: A common C4 mistake is to assume a container is:
questions.explanation: Beginners often equate "container" with "microservice". A container is any deployable unit — mobile apps, SPAs, databases, and batch jobs all qualify.
options: Always a microservice
The same as a UML class
A single source file
An AWS EC2 instance

questions.question: Which C4 level is most useful for explaining the system to a NON-technical stakeholder?
questions.explanation: Context treats the system as a black box surrounded by people and external systems — the clearest view for business stakeholders.
options: Code
Component
Container
Context

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the "Code" level in C4, and why is it often skipped?
questions.explanation: Code-level diagrams duplicate what modern IDEs show at a click. C4 recommends skipping them unless genuinely helpful.
options: To replace unit tests; it's skipped because tests suffice
To show classes/interfaces inside a component; it's skipped because IDEs already generate this on demand
To produce deployment diagrams; it's skipped because operations owns those
To act as a legal record of the architecture

questions.question: What philosophy does Simon Brown use to describe the C4 model?
questions.explanation: Brown describes C4 as "a map of your code, at different zoom levels" — emphasising that each level serves a different audience and conversation.
options: "One diagram to rule them all"
"A map of your code, at different zoom levels"
"Always use formal UML notation"
"Diagrams must be maintained by architects only"

questions.question: What does the C4 Context diagram show?
questions.explanation: Context is the outermost view: your system as a black box, surrounded by the actors and external systems that interact with it.
options: The classes inside the application
The system as a black box, plus the people and external systems it interacts with
The deployment infrastructure in detail
The release pipeline steps

questions.question: In C4, what does a "Component" represent?
questions.explanation: Components live inside containers and are the logical building blocks: modules, packages, named services. They are NOT the same as microservices.
options: A microservice
A cloud region
A building block inside a container — a module, package, or internal service
A type of user

questions.question: Who should be able to understand a C4 Context diagram without any prior technical training?
questions.explanation: The Context diagram is the most accessible level: simple enough that any stakeholder can understand who uses the system and what it connects to.
options: Only software architects
Only senior engineers
Only DevOps engineers
A new joiner or business stakeholder — it is designed for broad readability

questions.question: Which C4 level is frequently skipped because modern IDEs generate the same information on demand?
questions.explanation: The Code level (classes, interfaces) is often skipped because IDEs show this automatically. Maintaining a separate Code-level diagram rarely adds value.
options: Context
Container
Component
Code

questions.question: What do arrows in a C4 diagram represent?
questions.explanation: In C4, an arrow consistently means "depends on" or "calls." This consistent meaning is part of the notation's readability.
options: Only network traffic flows
Dependency or calling relationships — "A depends on / calls B"
Data volumes per second
Security boundaries

questions.question: C4 diagrams are deliberately NOT which type of formal notation?
questions.explanation: C4 favours plain readability over formal UML notation. A simple legend replaces the need to learn a standard notation.
options: Markdown
UML
JSON
YAML

questions.question: A team needs to explain their system to a new CTO with no technical background. Which C4 level should they use first?
questions.explanation: Context is the most accessible: the system as a black box, surrounded by users and external systems. Perfect for business stakeholders.
options: Code
Component
Container
Context

questions.question: A developer says "our C4 container diagram shows all 27 of our microservices." What is the likely problem?
questions.explanation: The confusion of "container = microservice" is common. More importantly, 27 items on one diagram often defeats C4's readability purpose.
options: Nothing — containers ARE microservices in C4
27 items on one diagram may defeat C4's readability goal; a C4 container is also not specifically a microservice
Microservices should only appear in the Component diagram
The diagram must be split by team ownership

questions.question: What specific problem do "diagrams-as-code" tools like Structurizr solve for C4?
questions.explanation: Diagrams-as-code in a repo ages with the code — when the architecture changes, the diagram can be regenerated. Diagrams in wikis drift silently.
options: They generate diagrams automatically from source code without any input
They keep diagrams version-controlled and regenerable from a single source, preventing silent staleness
They replace the need for architecture reviews
They enforce UML compliance

questions.question: A container diagram shows a web app, an API, a database, and a message queue. Which are correctly described as C4 "containers"?
questions.explanation: A C4 container is anything that runs: a web app, an API server, a database, a message queue, or a batch job all qualify.
options: Only the web app
Only the database
Only the API
All four — each is a deployable or executable unit

questions.question: The C4 Component level zooms inside which element?
questions.explanation: Component diagrams live inside a single container, showing its internal building blocks. You choose one container to zoom into at a time.
options: A person or external system in the Context diagram
A specific container
The entire system context
A code-level class

questions.question: Why does C4 advise to "be ruthless about what to leave out"?
questions.explanation: The value of C4 diagrams is their focus. Every element added for completeness reduces the diagram's usefulness for the conversation it is designed to support.
options: Diagrams must fit on a single A4 page by standard
Clarity comes from omission; including every detail recreates the spider-web diagrams C4 was designed to replace
There is a technical limit to C4 diagram size
Leaving things out protects intellectual property

questions.question: Which C4 diagram would you choose to show which technology stack runs in each deployable unit?
questions.explanation: The Container diagram shows the deployable/executable units, their technologies, and how they communicate — the right level for deployment and technology questions.
options: Context
Component
Container
Code

questions.question: The deep dive says most architecture diagrams "fail because they try to say everything on one page." What is the specific consequence?
questions.explanation: The "say everything" impulse produces diagrams that are unreadable and unmaintainable. C4's hierarchy solves this by giving each zoom level ONE job.
options: Legal liability for incorrect information
A spider web of boxes nobody can read that goes stale the day it is drawn
Too much information for the build system to parse
Expensive licensing costs for diagram tools

questions.question: According to the deep dive, which three explicit choices make C4 succeed?
questions.explanation: The deep dive names three design decisions: hierarchical abstraction (each diagram has one job), notation consistency (terms mean one thing), and living artifacts (diagrams-as-code).
options: Colour coding, icon libraries, and layered templates
Hierarchical abstraction, notation consistency, and living artefacts
XML schema, version numbers, and access controls
Simplicity, brevity, and formal review processes

questions.question: According to the deep dive, what is the key consequence of "notation consistency"?
questions.explanation: Consistent notation means "container" always means one thing and arrows always mean one thing. Once learned, the notation is universal across all C4 diagrams.
options: Every diagram looks visually identical
A reader learns the notation once and applies it everywhere — reducing the cognitive overhead of reading any C4 diagram
All diagrams must be drawn by the same person
Consistency is enforced by a linting tool

questions.question: A common C4 mistake is assuming "Container" and "Microservice" are synonyms. Why is this wrong?
questions.explanation: The term "container" is independent of microservices. It means "a thing that runs" — which includes apps, services, jobs, databases, and message buses.
options: Microservices don't run in containers
A container is any deployable unit — a mobile app, SPA, batch job, or database are all containers but not necessarily microservices
Microservices are shown at the Component level
Containers are only databases and message queues

questions.question: The deep dive states that "service boundaries show up at the COMPONENT level, if at all." What does this imply about the Container level?
questions.explanation: Container diagrams show "what runs and how they communicate." The decomposition into service boundaries is a Component-level concern, if it needs to be shown at all.
options: Container diagrams must show service boundaries explicitly
Container diagrams show deployable units and communication, not internal service boundary decisions
Service boundaries don't exist in C4 at any level
Component diagrams are only relevant for microservices

questions.question: What does "living artefact" mean for a C4 diagram maintained with Structurizr or PlantUML C4 extension?
questions.explanation: Diagrams-as-code means the diagram lives in the repo, is regenerable, and can be reviewed and updated in the same workflow as the code it describes.
options: The diagram updates automatically on every code deploy
The diagram is in source control, regenerable from the same model, so it can be updated when the architecture changes
The diagram has an expiry date and must be redrawn annually
The diagram is connected to a live production database

questions.question: A practical implication of "service boundaries show up at the COMPONENT level, if at all" is that Container diagrams should:
questions.explanation: Container diagrams are for deployment topology and technology choices. Showing internal service decomposition at this level adds noise rather than clarity.
options: List every microservice for completeness and accuracy
Focus on deployable units and their communication, not on internal decomposition decisions
Always be more important than Component diagrams
Show service boundaries as separate nested boxes

questions.question: Vertical Slice Architecture organises code primarily by:
questions.explanation: Each slice contains everything one feature needs — HTTP, validation, business logic, persistence — in one place.
options: Technical layer
Feature
Team
Programming language

questions.question: Who popularised Vertical Slice Architecture?
questions.explanation: Jimmy Bogard (author of MediatR and AutoMapper) wrote the seminal posts on vertical slices.
options: Eric Evans
Jimmy Bogard
Kent Beck
Uncle Bob

questions.question: In a traditional n-layer architecture, changing one feature typically means editing:
questions.explanation: Horizontal layering spreads one feature across every layer — vertical slices collapse that into a single folder.
options: A single file
One folder
Multiple files across multiple layer folders (Controllers, Services, Repositories, etc.)
Only the database

questions.question: Which of these is a real trade-off of Vertical Slice Architecture?
questions.explanation: Vertical slices intentionally accept some duplication to avoid the wrong shared abstraction. "A little duplication is cheaper than the wrong coupling."
options: It cannot be tested
Some code that would be shared in an n-layer design ends up duplicated across slices
It only works in Java
It removes the need for a database

questions.question: Vertical slices pair naturally with which pattern?
questions.explanation: Each slice is typically one command or one query handler — a CQRS-shaped unit of behaviour.
options: Singleton everywhere
CQRS — separate Command and Query handlers
Global mutable state
Inheritance over composition

questions.question: In vertical-slice parlance, what is meant by "tailored design per slice"?
questions.explanation: Vertical slices free you from forcing every feature through the same layered template. Design complexity goes where it earns its keep.
options: Each slice must use a different framework
Simple features stay simple; complex ones can add layers only where those layers genuinely help
Each slice needs its own database
Only senior developers can design a slice

questions.question: Why is CreateInvoice able to use a totally different design (e.g. event-sourced) from VoidInvoice in a vertical-slice codebase?
questions.explanation: Independence is the point: each slice is free to pick the design best suited to its feature, since slices don't funnel through a shared service layer.
options: Because the compiler enforces it
Because the two slices are independent — they do not share a central Service<Invoice> that couples them
Because Jimmy Bogard requires it
Because they use different programming languages

questions.question: Vertical Slice Architecture echoes which idea from Uncle Bob?
questions.explanation: Screaming Architecture: a new joiner reading the top-level folders should see "CreateInvoice, SendReceipt, RefundOrder" — the business — not "Controllers, Services, Repos".
options: The Repository Pattern
Screaming Architecture — the folder structure should scream what the system DOES, not what framework it uses
Dependency Injection as a religion
The Open/Closed Principle

questions.question: What is the relationship between vertical slices and MediatR-style "request/handler" libraries?
questions.explanation: MediatR's request→handler mapping naturally expresses "one feature, one handler", making vertical slices easy to implement.
options: MediatR is required by the vertical-slice pattern
MediatR (or equivalents) provide a clean way to pipe one request to one handler, matching the one-slice-one-feature shape
Vertical slices are only legal in C#
MediatR forces horizontal layering

questions.question: In a vertical-slice codebase, what does the folder name "CreateOrder/" immediately tell a developer?
questions.explanation: In vertical slices, folder names reflect business capabilities. "CreateOrder/" tells you what the feature does before you open a single file.
options: Which programming language is used
Which team owns the code
What business capability the feature implements
Which database table is involved

questions.question: What does the term "slice" refer to in Vertical Slice Architecture?
questions.explanation: A slice is a self-contained unit for one feature: it owns everything from the HTTP handler through validation, business logic, and persistence.
options: A network partition
A feature containing all the code it needs — from HTTP handler to database access
A horizontal layer of the application
A team boundary

questions.question: What makes it easier to DELETE a feature in a vertical-slice codebase?
questions.explanation: High cohesion and low coupling per slice means deleting a feature is as simple as removing its folder — nothing in other slices depends on it.
options: Because slices are always small in size
Because each feature is isolated in one folder with high cohesion and low coupling to unrelated features
Because there is no database involved
Because features are deployed as separate services

questions.question: What does "low coupling" mean in the context of vertical slices?
questions.explanation: Low coupling means unrelated features are independent — changes in one slice cannot accidentally break another.
options: Slices share absolutely no code with each other
Unrelated features cannot accidentally share state or constrain each other's design
Each slice has its own dedicated server
Slices only communicate via a REST API

questions.question: Which library does Jimmy Bogard maintain that enables the request/handler pattern commonly used in vertical slices?
questions.explanation: MediatR provides the request→handler pipeline that makes it easy to implement one-slice-one-handler in C# projects.
options: Entity Framework
AutoMapper only
MediatR
ASP.NET Core

questions.question: What is "high cohesion" in the context of a vertical slice?
questions.explanation: High cohesion means everything that belongs to one feature lives together — the command, handler, validator, and query are all in the same slice.
options: Everything about one feature is co-located in one place
All database code lives in one central folder
All HTTP handlers live in one central folder
All validators are grouped together

questions.question: Vertical Slice Architecture is most directly an alternative to which traditional approach?
questions.explanation: Vertical slices invert the n-layer split: instead of organising by technical layer, you organise by feature/business capability.
options: Domain-Driven Design
Microservices
Horizontal n-layer architecture (Controllers, Services, Repositories)
Event-driven architecture

questions.question: A team is adding a feature to a vertical-slice codebase. Which files are most likely to change?
questions.explanation: In vertical slices, a feature change touches only its own slice. No other folders need to open.
options: Controllers.cs, Services.cs, and Repositories.cs across multiple folders
Only the files within the single feature's slice folder
The shared BaseController and the ServiceRegistry
The entire persistence layer

questions.question: In a vertical-slice system, where does shared infrastructure like authentication or logging go?
questions.explanation: Shared infrastructure exists but is minimal and explicit — small "shared" modules that slices reference intentionally, not giant layers every slice inherits from.
options: It is duplicated in every slice
It lives in small explicit "shared" modules that slices consciously consume
It doesn't exist — each slice handles it independently
It goes in a giant horizontal layer at the top of the codebase

questions.question: What does Jimmy Bogard mean by "the wrong abstraction"?
questions.explanation: The wrong abstraction is one where unrelated features must share a design just to fit through a central layer — coupling them in ways that hurt both.
options: An abstraction that is too large for its purpose
A shared layer that forces unrelated features to conform to one design, creating accidental coupling
An abstraction written in the wrong programming language
An abstraction that is insufficiently documented

questions.question: How does a vertical-slice codebase "scream what the system does," in Uncle Bob's phrase?
questions.explanation: A new joiner reading "CreateOrder/, CancelOrder/, ShipOrder/" immediately understands the system's purpose — not its technical stack.
options: The code comments describe every business rule
The top-level folder structure reflects business capabilities rather than framework layers
The README lists all features explicitly
Class names use business terminology throughout

questions.question: What problem does a typical n-layer Service<Invoice> class create as the system grows?
questions.explanation: A central Service<Invoice> accumulates every invoice operation, making unrelated features depend on each other's constraints and side-effects.
options: It is too slow at runtime
It grows to handle ALL invoice scenarios, coupling unrelated features through one central class
It uses too much memory
It violates the Open/Closed Principle by definition

questions.question: Why does vertical-slice architecture consider some duplication acceptable?
questions.explanation: Forced sharing through an imperfect abstraction creates coupling that's harder to remove than duplicated code. VSA accepts the trade-off deliberately.
options: Because storage is cheap in modern cloud environments
Because a little duplication is less harmful than coupling features through the wrong shared abstraction
Because teams prefer simpler code overall
Because duplicated code is easier to test in isolation

questions.question: A new developer joins and sees top-level folders named "CreateOrder/", "CancelOrder/", "ShipOrder/". What do they immediately know?
questions.explanation: Feature-named folders communicate the system's purpose instantly — the "screaming architecture" benefit of vertical slices.
options: The technical stack the system uses
The business operations the system supports — they understand what the system does before reading any code
The database schema structure
The team's sprint history

questions.question: The deep dive says horizontal layering "optimises for the wrong thing." What does it actually optimise for?
questions.explanation: Horizontal layers look tidy on a diagram but optimise for that visual cleanliness, not for the actual axis of change: features.
options: Developer experience during feature work
Ease of drawing architecture diagrams
Runtime performance
Testing isolation

questions.question: Why can CreateInvoice use pure CRUD while VoidInvoice uses event-sourcing in a vertical-slice codebase?
questions.explanation: Independence is the point: each slice is free to pick the design best suited to its feature, since slices don't funnel through a shared service layer.
options: Because they use different frameworks
Because they are independent slices with no shared service layer constraining their design
Because CRUD and event-sourcing use different databases
Because the compiler enforces different patterns per folder

questions.question: According to the deep dive, what is the "axis of change" that vertical slices optimise for?
questions.explanation: Vertical slices align the code structure with the most common kind of change: adding, modifying, or removing a feature.
options: Changes to the technical stack
Feature changes — the unit of work is a feature, so the unit of code is also a feature
Database schema changes
Infrastructure changes

questions.question: What is the relationship between "Screaming Architecture" (Uncle Bob) and Vertical Slice Architecture?
questions.explanation: VSA is one concrete realisation of Screaming Architecture: a new joiner reads the folders and sees the business domain, not the framework.
options: They are unrelated concepts from different eras
Screaming Architecture says structure should reveal intent; VSA implements this by making top-level folders reflect business capabilities
Screaming Architecture requires vertical slices by definition
Uncle Bob invented vertical slices

questions.question: According to the deep dive, CQRS pairs well with VSA because:
questions.explanation: CQRS's request→handler shape maps directly to the one-slice-one-feature structure, making the two patterns highly complementary.
options: CQRS requires microservices, and VSA requires microservices
Each slice is typically one command or one query handler — a natural one-to-one mapping
CQRS mandates vertical slices in its specification
CQRS solves the duplication problem that VSA introduces

questions.question: Why does Jimmy Bogard argue that "a little duplication beats the wrong abstraction"?
questions.explanation: The cost of the wrong abstraction compounds over time as more features adapt to fit through it. Localised duplication stays localised and can be removed cleanly.
options: Duplication is always cheaper than abstraction
Forced sharing through an imperfect abstraction creates coupling that is harder to remove than duplicated code
Duplication is easier to test in isolation
The wrong abstraction can always be refactored easily later

questions.question: In the deep dive, what does "shared infrastructure" look like in a well-designed vertical-slice system?
questions.explanation: Shared modules exist but are small and explicit — not the dominant structure of the codebase. Slices reference them intentionally, not by default.
options: Placed in giant horizontal layers above each slice
Small, explicit "shared" modules that slices actively and consciously consume
Merged directly into every slice via copy-paste
It does not exist at all in a pure vertical-slice system

questions.question: What does ADR stand for?
questions.explanation: ADR stands for Architecture Decision Record — a short, numbered document capturing one significant architectural decision.
options: Application Deployment Record
Architecture Decision Record
Automated Data Recovery
Agile Delivery Roadmap

questions.question: Where do ADRs typically live?
questions.explanation: ADRs live next to the code they describe — usually in a docs/adr/ folder — so they're version-controlled and reviewed with the same workflow as the code.
options: Only in a shared confluence space nobody reads
In the repository alongside the code (e.g. docs/adr/)
In the architect's private notebook
On the company wiki, separate from the code

questions.question: Which section of a typical ADR captures "what becomes easier, harder, or riskier" after the decision?
questions.explanation: The Consequences section is where trade-offs are made explicit — arguably the most valuable part of an ADR for future readers.
options: Status
Context
Decision
Consequences

questions.question: What should you do when an accepted ADR no longer reflects the chosen architecture?
questions.explanation: ADRs are immutable. You write a new ADR that supersedes the old one, preserving the history of why the earlier decision was made.
options: Edit the original ADR to reflect the new decision
Delete the ADR so it does not confuse readers
Write a new ADR that supersedes it; mark the old one superseded
Move the ADR to an archive folder and start over

questions.question: Which of these is the best scope for a single ADR?
questions.explanation: Granularity matters: one ADR = one decision. Small, focused ADRs are easier to read, supersede, and search later.
options: One ADR covering all persistence, messaging, and auth decisions
One ADR per major quarter of work
One ADR per architectural decision
One ADR per microservice

questions.question: Why are ADRs usually append-only and never edited after acceptance?
questions.explanation: Immutability preserves the record of *why* a decision was made at a point in time — critical context when the world changes and a new ADR supersedes it.
options: File systems make editing hard
To preserve the history of thinking so future teams can understand why decisions were made
Because tooling requires it
To discourage people from ever revisiting decisions

questions.question: Who is generally credited with popularizing the lightweight ADR format?
questions.explanation: Michael Nygard proposed lightweight ADRs in his 2011 post "Documenting Architecture Decisions" as an alternative to heavyweight architecture docs.
options: Martin Fowler
Michael Nygard
Gregor Hohpe
Robert C. Martin

questions.question: Which statement best captures why ADRs pair naturally with "You build it, you run it"?
questions.explanation: Autonomous delivery teams benefit most when the "why" travels with the code — the same people who ship it live with the consequences and write them down.
options: Running systems require fewer decisions than building them
ADRs replace the need for runbooks
The team that owns the system also owns the record of why it is the way it is
Operational teams refuse to take over systems without ADRs

questions.question: What is the primary intent of the Status field on an ADR (proposed / accepted / superseded)?
questions.explanation: Status makes the lifecycle of a decision legible: readers can immediately see whether an ADR represents the current design or a chapter in its history.
options: To trigger an approval workflow in a ticket system
To let readers tell at a glance which decisions are current and which are history
To grant the author editing rights
To determine code review ownership

questions.question: Who is generally credited with proposing the lightweight ADR format in 2011?
questions.explanation: Michael Nygard proposed lightweight ADRs in his 2011 post "Documenting Architecture Decisions" as an alternative to heavyweight architecture documents.
options: Martin Fowler
Michael Nygard
Gregor Hohpe
Simon Brown

questions.question: Which of these is a valid ADR status?
questions.explanation: ADR statuses are: Proposed (under discussion), Accepted (current decision), and Superseded (replaced by a newer ADR).
options: Open, In Progress, Closed
Proposed, Accepted, Superseded
Draft, Review, Published
New, Active, Archived

questions.question: What does the "Context" section of an ADR capture?
questions.explanation: Context captures the background: the forces, constraints, and situation that made the decision necessary in the first place.
options: The code changes made to implement the decision
The forces in play that made the decision necessary
The team members involved in the discussion
The budget allocated for the decision

questions.question: What is the purpose of numbering ADRs sequentially?
questions.explanation: Sequential numbering gives each ADR a stable reference (e.g. "see ADR-0012") and makes the history of decisions easy to navigate.
options: To rank decisions by importance
To provide a unique identifier and show the chronological order of decisions
To allocate review bandwidth among team members
To set priority for implementation order

questions.question: An ADR's "Decision" section states:
questions.explanation: The Decision section is a clear statement of what was chosen — not the context or consequences, just the choice itself.
options: The problem background and forces in play
What was chosen, stated clearly and unambiguously
Who made the decision and when
When the decision will next be reviewed

questions.question: How long is a typical ADR supposed to be?
questions.explanation: ADRs are intentionally one page: short enough to actually be written during the decision, and read by future team members.
options: 10–20 pages with full design rationale
One page — short and focused on one decision
As long as needed for comprehensive documentation
3–5 pages covering all related decisions

questions.question: What problem do ADRs solve six months after a decision is made?
questions.explanation: Without ADRs, the reasoning behind past decisions is lost. New joiners re-open old debates; teams waste time second-guessing well-considered choices.
options: They automate rollback of bad decisions
They preserve the "why" behind decisions so future teams can understand, re-evaluate, or intentionally replace them
They measure the quality of architectural decisions
They enforce consistency across teams

questions.question: A team discovers that ADR-005 (use REST APIs) is no longer appropriate as they now need event-driven communication. The correct action is:
questions.explanation: ADRs are immutable. Write a new ADR referencing the old one, mark the old one superseded, and preserve the full history of the thinking.
options: Edit ADR-005 to change it to event-driven
Delete ADR-005 and create a fresh replacement
Write a new ADR that supersedes ADR-005 and mark ADR-005 as superseded
Archive ADR-005 in a separate folder without a replacement

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates why ADRs prevent "reopening old debates"?
questions.explanation: The ADR acts as institutional memory: the new joiner gets the full context of the decision without needing to gather it from people who may have left.
options: A new team member asks "why PostgreSQL?" — the ADR gives the context, options considered, and trade-offs accepted at the time
The CTO has an excellent memory for past decisions
A ticketing system tracks which decisions were made
All team members were present when every decision was made

questions.question: Why is the Consequences section more valuable than the Decision section for future readers?
questions.explanation: Future readers need to know what the decision constrains, enables, and risks — not just what was chosen, but what living with it means.
options: Because the decision is usually obvious in hindsight
Because consequences show what trade-offs were accepted, helping future teams understand what they are working within
Because the decision section is usually incorrect
Because consequences are easier and faster to write

questions.question: Who should ideally write an ADR, according to the deep dive?
questions.explanation: ADRs work best when written by the people making the decision, capturing live context — not delegated to a separate documentation role.
options: Only the chief architect
Anyone making the decision — architect, tech lead, or the team itself
A dedicated technical writing team
The project manager after the decision is finalised

questions.question: A team writes "We chose PostgreSQL AND Redis AND Kafka" in a single ADR. What is wrong with this?
questions.explanation: Small, focused ADRs are easier to read, easier to supersede individually, and easier to search for later. One decision per ADR is the rule.
options: Nothing — comprehensive ADRs are more useful
It violates the "one ADR = one decision" principle; these should be three separate ADRs
Using three technologies is too complex for a single system
Kafka is not an architectural decision

questions.question: When is the ideal time to write an ADR?
questions.explanation: Writing during the meeting captures the actual options, the live trade-off reasoning, and the real context — all of which erode quickly after the fact.
options: A week after the decision, when the dust has settled
During the decision meeting itself — as a working document capturing live context
During the annual architecture review
After the feature implementing the decision has shipped

questions.question: What does "append-only" mean for an ADR repository?
questions.explanation: Append-only preserves the full historical record. The sequence of ADRs tells the story of how the architecture evolved and why.
options: You can only add text to an ADR, never delete any
New information or changed decisions require a new ADR; old ADRs are never edited
ADRs are stored in append-only databases
Only one person can contribute to each ADR

questions.question: According to the deep dive, a "retrospective artefact" ADR (filled in after the fact) is inferior because:
questions.explanation: The value of an ADR is its capture of live thinking. Written retrospectively, it becomes a rationalisation rather than a record of what was actually considered.
options: It is harder to format correctly
It loses the live context, options considered, and reasoning that only exist during the actual decision moment
The team has already forgotten all the alternatives by then
Retrospective ADRs are always too long

questions.question: Why does ADR immutability specifically preserve the history of thinking?
questions.explanation: The sequence of ADRs and their superseding relationships shows how the architecture evolved — which is impossible to reconstruct if old ADRs are overwritten.
options: Because immutable files physically cannot be deleted
Because future readers can see what was true at the time of each decision and why each subsequent ADR was necessary
Because git history alone is insufficient for this purpose
Because regulations require it

questions.question: The deep dive says "Consequences matter more than the decision." What evidence supports this claim?
questions.explanation: The decision is history; the consequences are what future teams live with. Acknowledging trade-offs explicitly prevents the ADR from pretending a silver bullet was found.
options: The Consequences section is always shorter and therefore easier to scan
Writing consequences forces the author to acknowledge trade-offs — the information future readers most need
Consequences are more factual than decisions and therefore more reliable
Consequences are the only section that cannot be superseded

questions.question: Why were lightweight ADRs proposed as an alternative to heavyweight architecture documents?
questions.explanation: A 50-page architecture document no-one reads provides no value. A one-page ADR that teams actually write, read, and refer to provides compounding value.
options: Lightweight documents are always preferable to heavyweight ones
Heavyweight docs become outdated quickly and are rarely read; lightweight ADRs stay small enough to remain current and useful
ADRs require less formal formatting than architecture documents
Architects simply prefer shorter documents

questions.question: ADR-022 has status "superseded by ADR-037." What status does ADR-037 most likely carry?
questions.explanation: ADR-037 supersedes ADR-022, so it should be the currently accepted decision. Accepted means it represents the current architectural choice.
options: Also superseded by a later ADR
Proposed — it is still under discussion
Accepted — it is the current active decision
Archived — it is no longer relevant

questions.question: How do ADRs complement "You build it, you run it" specifically?
questions.explanation: YBYR gives teams end-to-end ownership. ADRs ensure the "why" travels with that ownership — the team is accountable for both the decisions and their consequences.
options: They reduce the number of deployment decisions a team must make
The team that owns and operates the system also owns the record of why it was built that way — accountability follows the code
They automate operational decision-making
ADRs replace runbooks for common operational procedures

questions.question: What distinguishes an ADR written as a "working document" from one written retrospectively?
questions.explanation: A working document is a live record of the decision process. A retrospective one reconstructs it from memory — losing the options that were rejected and the reasoning that was live.
options: Working documents are always longer and more detailed
Working documents capture the actual options and reasoning as they existed during the decision; retrospective ones often rationalise choices after the fact
Working documents require more formal approvals
Working documents use a different template structure
